description:
Central ledger for the ancora 1.0 friction found in real consumer work. One day of Atlas sessions (2026-09-03, six Claude sessions plus headless cx workers) produced every finding below. CI paints green; the transcripts show that green was bought with human rulings, worker bounces, hand-ported gates, and retried flakes. This ticket is the single place to investigate each partition deeply, decide what ancora should actually do, and spawn properly scoped fix tickets as children. No fix lands on this ticket directly.

Evidence sources, cited per item below:
- Session transcripts under /Users/mz/.claude-remembers/projects/-Users-mz-dev-mz-atlas/: 98be5781 (atlas-1f8 ship), 85679cb0 (atlas-3mu implement), 5c32bee7 + 542ec4c7 (atlas-woc review/ship), 7f2b6af7 (atlas-3mu plan), e1c60338.
- Atlas migration record: ancora-yzu.25 IMPLEMENTED comment (2026-09-03T02:05:58Z) and the migration ADR .spec/decisions/atlas.decision.ancora_1_0_migration.md on Atlas main.
- Atlas CI runs 33706541743 (main red at the migration commit cec83a14b), 33766153417, 33738621304.

== A. Gate soundness: false greens (the gate certifies what it did not check) ==

A1. Tag borrowing is invisible. A test can tag any requirement id and ancora counts the requirement verified, with no check that the test asserts anything the requirement describes. Observed: new is_file/hint behavior anchored by a test tagged mcp.code_access_tools.unified_universe; reviewer verdict verbatim: "Ancora cannot catch this — the gate is green at errors=0 warnings=0 — so review is the only control." (5c32bee7 at 11:44Z and 11:51Z, atlas board ticket woc review.) Investigate: what signal is even computable here (mutation sampling? binding overlap between the test's reached functions and the subject's footprint?), and what the honest limit of static checking is.

A2. append/must_downgraded misses prose drift. It detects priority downgrades only; statement narrowing or widening sails through, and the Atlas epic "repeatedly found spec prose still asserting behavior the code no longer has" (85679cb0 at 21:13Z, follow-up filed on the atlas board as narrowed-prose debt). The append-only guard family protects the wrong axis for this failure mode. Investigate: whether requirement-text change classification (semantic, not just presence/absence) is feasible, or whether the answer is a review-artifact affordance instead of a finding.

A3. Acknowledgment durability. Spec-Ack trailers are destroyed by squash merges ([ancora-sfu](https://github.com/iautom8things/ancora/blob/beadwork/issues/ancora-sfu.json)) and hidden by shallow clones ([ancora-11w](https://github.com/iautom8things/ancora/blob/beadwork/issues/ancora-11w.json)). Already filed; listed here because any redesign in partition B likely lands on the same vocabulary, so they should be planned together, not patched separately.

== B. Gate soundness: false or unactionable reds ==

B1. change/missing_decision is path-set only. missing_decision?/1 (lib/ancora/policy_files.ex) fires when any governance path changes and no .spec/decisions/ file changes in the same diff. It cannot see that a governing decision already exists at base. Cost on 2026-09-03: an atlas-3mu.3 worker hit three unclearable warnings, posted WORKER_ERROR, received a wrong orchestrator ruling asserting frontmatter references clear it, read the installed source, pushed back, and was proven right; the ruling was retracted (85679cb0 at 20:11-20:14Z). A finding that a correct diff cannot clear except by touching an unrelated decision file teaches people to make noise edits. Investigate: what "the change is already governed" should mean and how to detect it.

B2. derived/drift fan-out on shared bindings. One epic rebased onto the migration produced spec.check result=fail errors=46, all derived/drift, spanning 25 subjects whose contracts did not change, because seven shared functions (Telemetry.metrics/0, Inventory entry points, Manifest.ensure/3) sit in many subjects' footprints (98be5781 at 03:02Z). Resolution required interrupting Manuel for a policy ruling and a Spec-Ack derived/drift=info trailer on the release commit (answered 08:22Z). Every epic touching a shared function replays this. Investigate: whether drift on a subject should distinguish "the changed function's own subject" from "reached transitively," whether acknowledgment should scope to a binding rather than a code, and what the right blast-radius model is.

B3. Unclearable finding from config shape. Trailing slash in lib_paths makes change/uncovered_file unclearable because two path-boundary rules disagree ([ancora-ufm](https://github.com/iautom8things/ancora/blob/beadwork/issues/ancora-ufm.json), filed). Same class as B1: a red the user cannot legitimately clear.

== C. Expressiveness gaps (consumers are hand-rolling what ancora dropped) ==

C1. No command verification kind. specled had kind: command (repo grep gates). Ancora 1.0 dropped it; Atlas lost two working gates in the migration (no tier tokens in retrieval, no payload bytes in code-access logs), one requirement fell to requirement_unverified, and consumers now hand-port each gate to an ExUnit source-scan test. The pattern "Ancora 1.0 has no command kind, so the gate is an ExUnit source scan" appears in three sessions the same day, including the next epic's plan, so it is now load-bearing convention (98be5781 at 08:25Z; 7f2b6af7 at 16:16Z; 85679cb0). Investigate: reinstate a command kind, or bless the ExUnit source-scan pattern officially (scaffold + docs) so every consumer stops reinventing it.

C2. Override grammar scopes to a subject, not a requirement. Atlas needed to override one blocked requirement (S5, enforce-flip gated) and had to override the whole mcp.code_access_tools subject, wider than intended, with a "remove when S5 lands" note (98be5781 at 08:46Z). Investigate: requirement-scoped overrides.

== D. Performance (known, quantified, unfixed) ==

All five Atlas budgets missed, median-of-3 on a warm build, 216 subjects / 2086 requirements: spec.check 37.2s (<10s budget), prime 31.9s, next 20.0s, status 16.9s, validate 10.3s (<5s each). Recorded in the migration ADR with the merge-now ruling. Fix is the on-disk OID cache [ancora-u38](https://github.com/iautom8things/ancora/blob/beadwork/issues/ancora-u38.json), blocked behind [ancora-xla](https://github.com/iautom8things/ancora/blob/beadwork/issues/ancora-xla.json) child xla.3. This partition needs no investigation, only prioritization: 30-second gates change how often people run the gate at all.

== E. Consumer collateral (not ancora defects; kept as the cost record) ==

E1. The Atlas trunk flake everyone sees. Egress-gate scan-budget test dies with :gate_down in CI, 3 of 3, first red on main at the migration commit cec83a14b (0.60.0 was green). Mechanism is Atlas's own 5s GenServer.call timeout conflated with gate death under coveralls load; the migration's added compile and retagged suites tipped the load. Tracked on the atlas board ([atlas-5wi](https://github.com/ChapterSpot/atlas/blob/beadwork/issues/atlas-5wi.json)); it now consumes a retry in most Atlas CI runs. Ancora is the trigger, not the cause. Relevance here: migration-driven load shifts are a real migration cost and belong in the migration checklist.

E2. Info-severity findings are un-auditable in practice. When a Spec-Ack's suppression needed enumeration, the 1900 hidden info findings could not be listed because Atlas's spec-check make target does not forward ANCORA_SHOW_INFO into the container (85679cb0 at 18:18Z). Atlas-side gap, but ancora's info-hiding default plus per-consumer plumbing means "what did this ack actually suppress" is routinely unanswerable. Consider a first-class ack-audit output.

E3. Brownfield noise budget. The migration left 1428 requirement_unverified at info, needed 53 test-tag remediations (37 retargets, 16 drops with ADR history), and 17 uncovered-file false positives (since fixed by the lib_paths change in ancora main 7511407). Baseline for judging whether future migrations get cheaper.

== How this ticket runs ==

1. Investigation first: each of A, B, C gets a deep-dive (reproduce in a fixture repo, read the relevant ancora internals, write findings as comments here).
2. Then a fix plan per partition, argued against the evidence above, with the durability items (A3) and vocabulary redesign (B2) planned together.
3. Fixes become child tickets; this ticket stays the ledger and closes when every partition is either fixed via a child or explicitly declined with reasoning recorded here.
4. D needs no investigation; unblocking u38 is a prioritization call to make during planning.

# Partition A — Gate soundness: false greens (ancora-gg8)

File refs are into /Users/mz/src/ancora unless prefixed.

## A1. Tag borrowing is invisible

### Root cause

The entire binding between a test and a requirement is string equality of an id.

- Ancora.TagScanner extracts literal `@tag spec:` / `@moduletag` / `@describetag` ids from test ASTs (lib/ancora/tag_scanner.ex:323-359). It records where a tag sits, never what the test asserts.
- Ancora.TagFindings checks exactly two things about that id: it exists in the corpus (`tags/unknown_requirement`, lib/ancora/tag_findings.ex:57-84) and every requirement has at least one tag (`tags/requirement_untagged`, lib/ancora/tag_findings.ex:86-104). Diff-scoped, `tags/new_requirement_untagged` adds "a NEW requirement must gain a tag in the same diff" (lib/ancora/change_analysis.ex:47-77). That is the complete vocabulary.
- The footprint machinery cannot help as built, because it is subject-granular, not requirement-granular. TagScanner.fold_to_subjects/1 (lib/ancora/tag_scanner.ex:83-106) lifts every requirement tag to its parent subject; Gate.subject_files/2 (lib/ancora/gate.ex:280-285) groups test files per subject; Derive.run unions all their resolved calls into one per-subject binding set (lib/ancora/derive.ex:148-167); Compare diffs that set base-vs-head for drift/growth/shrink. A requirement has no footprint of its own, so "does this test reach anything this requirement describes" is not even a well-formed question inside the current data model.

So a test tagged with any existing requirement id silences `requirement_untagged` and `new_requirement_untagged`, feeds the subject's footprint (silencing `change/uncovered_file` for the files it touches), and no code in the closed 30-code registry (lib/ancora/finding.ex:42-73) can fire.

### Grounded evidence

Atlas branch fix/list-files-path-is-file, review session 5c32bee7 (2026-09-03, ~11:44-11:51Z). New `is_file`/`hint` response keys were anchored by tests tagged `mcp.code_access_tools.unified_universe` (/Users/mz/dev/mz/atlas/test/atlas/code_access/code_access_test.exs:294, :675, :852), a requirement about manifest-universe visibility (/Users/mz/dev/mz/atlas/.spec/specs/mcp.code_access_tools.spec.md:43) that says nothing about hints. Consolidated review finding F5:

> "The current tag is dishonest: `complete/4` builds no clone ... so there is no clone-versus-manifest contrast for the test to assert, and the mutation that fails it is deleting the hint, not anything `unified_universe` describes. Ancora cannot catch this — the gate is green at errors=0 warnings=0 — so review is the only control."

The gate run in that session: checked subjects=216 requirements=2102 errors=0 warnings=0, result=pass (11:33Z). The reviewer called this "at least the fourth instance of this shape in this repo's review history" (prior instances: execute:true stubs, a path-normalization suite tagged to a git-diff-deletion requirement that "describes nothing of the sort", a preset-snapshot test that "passes under any implementation, inflating apparent coverage"). The spec reviewer named the mechanism exactly: "no code in Ancora's closed registry can fire here. tags/unknown_requirement cannot fire because the id exists, and spec/requirement_unverified cannot fire because the requirement already has other covering tests."

### What signal is computable, and what honestly is not

Honest limit first: static analysis can prove a test *reaches* code, never that its assertions *constrain* the behavior the prose describes. Prose semantics have exactly one mechanical oracle — mutation testing — and the atlas workflow already runs that oracle with LLM verifier agents (session 85679cb0, ~21:13Z: verify-3mu2-r2 decided three bounce items "each by a single-site mutation"). A static gate does not get to claim that ground.

Candidate directions:

1. **Diff-scoped borrowed-tag finding** (the reviewer's own proposal, refined): when a diff adds a `@tag spec:` naming a requirement id that pre-exists the diff and whose statement lines are untouched in the same diff, emit an info-tier finding ("tag binds new test to unchanged requirement X; confirm the test exercises it"). All inputs exist: base and head tag maps are both already scanned (lib/ancora/gate.ex:86-87), and ChangeAnalysis already does diff-scoped set comparisons. One new registry code, ~50 lines. Must stay info: backfilling coverage for an existing requirement is legitimate and encouraged, so this is a review pointer, not a violation — but it fires at the only moment anyone has context to judge the binding.
2. **Intra-requirement footprint overlap**: per-file call sets exist before the subject-level union (lib/ancora/derive.ex:152), so you could compare a new test's resolved calls against the union of the requirement's incumbent covering tests and flag near-zero overlap. Medium cost, noisy in the honest direction (a new facet legitimately reaches new functions), and the atlas F5 test would plausibly PASS it (it calls CodeAccess.list/2 like its neighbors). I would not build it.
3. **Mutation sampling in the gate**: needs a requirement-to-code binding that does not exist, answers "is this test falsifiable" rather than "does it verify this requirement," and costs compile+run per mutant. Over-engineering; it belongs to the review/verifier tier where it already lives and works.

Recommendation: option 1 only, at info. The tag is and stays a cooperative self-report (the Trailer moduledoc already says this about acks, lib/ancora/trailer.ex:19-23 — same epistemology). The gate's honest job is to make the self-report visible in the diff, not to pretend to validate semantics. A `mix spec.review` affordance listing the diff's new/changed tag bindings beside the requirement statements would hand reviewers the exact table they currently rebuild by hand.

## A2. append/must_downgraded misses prose drift

### Root cause

Ancora.AppendOnly.analyze/2 detects exactly two events (lib/ancora/append_only.ex:36-69): a requirement id present at base and absent at head, and priority must→should (must_to_should?/2, lib/ancora/append_only.ex:67-69). Its internal model keeps only {id, subject_id, priority} per requirement (lib/ancora/append_only.ex:105-130) — the statement field is dropped before any comparison. Rewriting a must's statement from "rejects all X" to "rejects X when flagged" is structurally invisible.

It is worse than a blind spot, because statement edits are *rewarded*: Ancora.Derive.Ack.substantive?/2 (lib/ancora/derive/ack.ex:14-21) returns true whenever the requirements or scenarios YAML differs after whitespace collapse, and the gate then suppresses that subject's derived/drift, derived/growth, and derived/shrink wholesale (lib/ancora/gate.ex:139-145, per requirement ancora.gate.acknowledgment_clears, .spec/specs/ancora.gate.spec.md:71). The same prose edit the guard cannot see also silences the footprint findings for its subject — and that acknowledgment event appears nowhere in the output. "Substantive" in the code means "different bytes," not "meaningful."

### Grounded evidence

Implement session 85679cb0 (atlas-3mu, ~21:13Z), filing the tier_gate prose follow-up ticket:

> "spec prose still asserting behavior the code no longer has, and the gate does not catch it. Ancora append/must_downgraded detects priority downgrades, not statement narrowing or widening. The prose is now slightly broader than the code."

### What is computable

Classifying a statement change as narrowing vs. widening is a natural-language judgment. No diff heuristic does it honestly — modal-verb stem comparison (adjacent machinery exists in lib/ancora/overlap.ex:134-149) would misclassify routinely and lend false authority. Don't.

What is computable, cheaply and exactly: "requirement X's statement changed in this diff." AppendOnly already walks both indexes by requirement id; keep the statement in its model and compare normalized strings. Emit an info-tier diff-scoped finding (e.g. append/statement_changed) naming the changed requirement ids. That does two things at once: prose drift stops being invisible (a reviewer or agent gets a finite "the contract text moved here, read it" list), and the currently-silent Ack event becomes visible — today the edit that clears a subject's drift findings is itself unreported.

Recommendation: review-artifact affordance, not a blocking finding. Info severity, one registry code, reusing AppendOnly's walk. Anything that *judges* the text change is over-engineering that converts honest "look here" into dishonest verdicts. The other direction (code changed, prose stale) is what derived/drift already covers; the gap is only the edited-prose direction.

## A3. Spec-Ack trailer durability

### Root cause

Acknowledgments live in the one place git workflows routinely rewrite or truncate: commit messages. Trailer.read/2 shells `git log <base>..HEAD --format=%B` and unions trailers across the range (lib/ancora/trailer.ex:56-61); Gate.resolve_findings/3 applies them as severity downgrades (lib/ancora/gate.ex:348-355). Two documented destruction modes:

- **Squash merge (ancora-sfu)**: epic commits 26e3100/c9d1efe carried `Spec-Ack: change/uncovered_file=info`; the PR squash-merged as 5d9cb40; main then had zero trailers, and spec.check on main went warnings=31 result=fail on findings that passed one commit earlier. No code change, no warning. Squash is the fleet's default merge strategy.
- **Shallow clone (ancora-11w)**: same commit a47d0fe, same command: full clone info=38 result=pass; GitHub runner at fetch-depth 1, warning=31 result=fail. Identical finding set, opposite verdicts, silent — truncated git log returns whatever history exists, and Trailer.read's error branch returns empty overrides with no diagnostic (lib/ancora/trailer.ex:59). No shallow detection exists anywhere in lib/ (grep confirms).

The moduledoc records the trajectory: HEAD-only scanning was widened to range scanning because "CI often sees squash or merge commits where the trailer lives one commit deep" (lib/ancora/trailer.ex:13-18). Range scanning moved the fragility rather than removing it. Structurally: an acknowledgment is durable, reviewable gate state, and commit metadata is neither durable (squash) nor reliably present (shallow), while the verdict depends on it.

### Rulings already made — do not re-litigate

Both tickets carry Manuel's rulings (comments, 2026-09-03T16:41Z):

- **ancora-sfu**: the durable record is the tree — .spec/config.yml severities and per-subject overrides. The trailer is demoted to a development convenience. spec.check must warn impossible-to-miss when a resolved acknowledgment exists only in a non-tip commit trailer. Explicitly: do NOT read the merge commit body. Document the promotion step.
- **ancora-11w**: hard env-tier failure at preflight when the base..HEAD range is not fully present locally, checked against the actual range (a shallow repo that still holds the whole range passes). Remedy names `git fetch --unshallow` / `fetch-depth: 0`. Lands on ancora-xla.2's env-tier routing. No named finding, no continue-with-warning.

Both fit the existing design (config.yml is already the reviewable severity record; preflight already hard-fails env problems as data, lib/ancora/gate/preflight.ex:5).

### Design space for partition B (binding-scoped acks)

1. **Where an ack lives**: (a) commit trailers — zero friction, zero durability, now demoted by ruling; (b) config.yml severities/overrides — durable, reviewed as a diff, but keyed by finding code and repo/subject-global; (c) in-spec per-requirement/per-binding ack blocks — durable, scoped, visible next to the thing acknowledged. A binding-scoped vocabulary wants (c) or a scoped extension of (b), and must not reintroduce (a) for anything long-lived.
2. **Granularity**: a trailer override is keyed by finding CODE (lib/ancora/trailer.ex:38, applied in lib/ancora/severity.ex:152-163), so `Spec-Ack: change/uncovered_file=info` downgraded all 31 uncovered-file findings, not the one being acknowledged. That is itself a false-green generator: acknowledging one instance silences every instance of the code in the range. The durable store must carry scope (code + file/requirement/binding), which config.yml's flat severities map cannot express today.
3. **Lifecycle**: a durable ack needs an expiry story or it becomes a permanent silence (the exact degeneration A2 shows in miniature, where "acknowledged" already means merely "edited"). Cheapest honest option: an ack names the finding instance it clears, and spec.check reports an ack whose target no longer fires as stale.
4. **Loudness at the boundary**: per the sfu ruling, the trailer path's remaining job is detection — "this run's verdict depends on a trailer that will not survive merge" must be impossible to miss. The 11w preflight check removes the other silent input (missing history) entirely.

Over-engineering warnings the rulings already closed: reading merge-commit bodies, trailer signing/authorship verification, any scheme making commit metadata durable. The tree is the record.

## Summary for an architect

All three findings are one disease at different layers: the gate treats a cooperative self-report as evidence and stays silent exactly where the self-report breaks down. A1 — the only test-to-requirement binding is id string equality, so a borrowed tag is unfalsifiable by construction; the data model has no requirement-level footprint to check against, and semantic verification genuinely belongs to mutation-running reviewers, not a static gate. A2 — the append guard models a requirement as {id, priority}, so statement edits are invisible, while the Ack mechanism simultaneously rewards any edit by silencing drift for the whole subject. A3 — acks live in commit messages, which squash destroys and shallow clones hide, producing opposite verdicts on the same commit with zero diagnostics; the rulings (already made) move the record into the tree and hard-fail incomplete history.

The cheap, honest fixes share one shape: stop adjudicating, start disclosing. Info-tier diff-scoped findings for "new test binds to unchanged requirement" and "requirement statement changed," make the ack event visible, refuse to run on incomplete history. Resist the heavy versions — footprint overlap scoring, prose-change classification, in-gate mutation testing — each trades the gate's current honest silence for confident wrongness, and the review tier already runs the only real oracle (mutation) where it belongs. Partition B's binding-scoped acks should land in the tree with instance-level scope and a staleness check; the code-keyed trailer downgrade is itself a false-green generator worth retiring for anything durable.

# Partition B — gate soundness: false or unactionable reds

## B1. change/missing_decision is path-set only

### Root cause

`Ancora.PolicyFiles.missing_decision?/1` at `lib/ancora/policy_files.ex:114-117`:

```elixir
def missing_decision?(changed_paths) when is_list(changed_paths) do
  Enum.any?(changed_paths, &governance?/1) and not Enum.any?(changed_paths, &decision_file?/1)
end
```

The whole rule is two set-membership checks over the diff's path list. It cannot see that a governing decision already exists at base, and no property of the changed content can clear it. `change_analysis.ex:37-45` emits one warning per changed governance file, the registry default is `warning` (`finding.ex:50`), and `spec.check` fails on warnings. The only clearing moves are touching any ADR file in the same diff, `Spec-Ack: change/missing_decision=info`, or a config severity.

The irony: ancora already parses both halves of a real governance linkage and uses neither here. Subject spec frontmatter has a `decisions:` list of ADR ids (`lib/ancora/schema/meta.ex:12`, consumed only by review HTML at `review.ex:151`), and ADRs have `affects:` with full resolution machinery in `lib/ancora/decision_parser/affects.ex` (resolvable-id collection at lines 109-118). In the atlas corpus, 199 of 216 subject specs carry a `decisions:` reference.

### Evidence (transcript 85679cb0, 2026-09-03 ~20:12-20:16Z)

Worker S3 hit three unclearable missing_decision warnings. The orchestrator ruled that appending the decision id to each spec's frontmatter `decisions:` list clears them; the worker refused, read the installed dep source, and won: "I was wrong and the worker was right. The gate is purely path-based: it requires a decision file in the same diff, and frontmatter references cannot satisfy it" (line 1656). The resolution was exactly the noise edit the rule incentivizes, a "dated, substantive addendum to the epic's own decision record" per stage. The orchestrator's summary shows the rule fires on luck: "S1 passed cleanly only because its diff happened to carry four decision files; S2 and S3 carry none, so both were always going to hit this" and "Three stages have now needed a file their ticket forbade" (line 1733).

### What "already governed" should mean; candidates

The incident's shape: an epic ADR already authorizes these subjects, workers edit their specs stage by stage, and every stage whose diff happens not to touch an ADR file gets flagged. "Already governed" = the changed spec is traceably under an ADR that resolves in the index.

1. **Bidirectional frontmatter linkage clears it (recommended).** Per changed subject spec, suppress when its `decisions:` (at HEAD) names an ADR that resolves in the current index and whose `affects:` names the subject (or a requirement/scenario in it) back. Frontmatter-less governance files (config.yml, AGENTS.md, README.md) keep the co-change rule. No new plumbing: `ChangeAnalysis.findings/5` already receives the current index. Tradeoff: an epic ADR authorizes repeat edits to its subjects while it stands, weakening the "every governance shift gets a fresh decision" ideal — but that ideal is already dead in practice, producing dated-addendum noise and passing S1 on luck. Notably everyone in the incident, orchestrator included, believed this was the semantics already.
2. **Only a newly added `decisions:` reference clears it** (diff base vs head frontmatter). More teeth, but re-flags every later stage of a multi-stage epic, which is the incident again. Skip.
3. **Staleness windows / ADR status gating.** Over-engineering, no evidence of need. Skip.

## B2. derived/drift fan-out on shared bindings

### Root cause

Drift is computed per subject over that subject's full transitive derived set. gate.ex:134-153 calls Compare.compare/4 once per subject; drift_findings (lib/ancora/derive/compare.ex:83-114) keeps every binding textually present on both sides, filters to those whose defining module's file changed (changed_definition?/3, compare.ex:144-153), and emits derived/drift per drifted binding. The `seen` dedup key {module, name, base_norm, head_norm} (compare.ex:125) is scoped inside one subject's call, so one changed shared function repeats once per subject that reaches it. Nothing in the pipeline models a binding's own subject.

Both clearing mechanisms mismatch the fan-out shape. Per-subject acknowledgment (gate.ex:139, lib/ancora/derive/ack.ex) requires a substantive requirements/scenarios edit to each subject's spec — 25 fake edits, and the finding text instructs exactly that ("edit the spec for this subject in the same diff", compare.ex:77-79). The Spec-Ack trailer (lib/ancora/trailer.ex) scopes to a finding code across the whole base..HEAD range, so `Spec-Ack: derived/drift=info` downgrades every drift finding in the diff, including any genuinely meaningful one a later commit in the range introduces.

### B2 evidence (transcript 98be5781, 2026-09-03)

At 03:02Z: `spec.check result=fail tier=branch errors=46 warnings=2`, all 46 derived/drift, collapsing to seven changed functions. From the worker's report (line 7716): "AtlasWeb.Telemetry.metrics/0 — 26 subjects", Inventory.fetch/4 — 6, entry_from_paths/1 — 6, Manifest.ensure/3 — 5, three singles. "The drifted subjects are ones whose tagged tests reach those functions but whose contracts our epic never touched … Every subject we did edit reports no drift." "Editing 25 unrelated subject specs to clear drift is out; it would be fake contract churn." Resolved at 08:22Z when Manuel answered AskUserQuestion with "Spec-Ack trailer on the release commit". The pipeline sat blocked 5h20m on a human severity ruling for a change that was, by the gate's own accounting, drift-free on every subject actually touched.

### B2 blast-radius quantification (atlas corpus)

All 216 atlas subjects declare `surface:` in spec-meta (216/216 by grep). lib/atlas_web/telemetry.ex appears in exactly 6 subjects' surface lists (access.workforce_sync, atlas.metrics_pipeline, atlas.platform_instrumentation, atlas.llm_instrumentation, atlas.sentry, mcp.observability) versus the 26 subjects that reached Telemetry.metrics/0 transitively in the incident. A primary/transitive split cuts that binding from 26 errors to 6, and those 6 are the plausible audience. Like `decisions:` in B1, `surface:` is parsed (schema/meta.ex:11) and used by nothing in the gate.

### B2 candidate directions

1. Primary/transitive severity split via `surface:` (recommended). A drift finding is primary when the drifted binding's defining file (already computed — defining_file/2, compare.ex:155-166) appears in the subject's surface list; otherwise emit a second registry code, derived/drift_transitive, defaulting to info. Two codes keep the closed registry, and config severities, per-subject overrides, and Spec-Ack trailers all compose for free because every existing mechanism keys on code. The 46-error incident becomes 6 errors on subjects whose declared code actually changed. Subjects without surface treat all drift as primary, so corpora that never authored it get the status quo.
2. Aggregate per binding: one finding per drifted binding listing the reached subjects instead of one per (subject, binding). Honest about what actually drifted (the function, not 25 contracts), cheap group-by in gate.ex — but it loses the per-subject ack/override wiring. Presentation-layer complement to 1, not a substitute.
3. Binding-scoped trailer acks (e.g. `Spec-Ack: derived/drift=info@AtlasWeb.Telemetry.metrics/0`). Surgical, but grows the trailer grammar, requires findings to carry a stable printable binding identity, and mechanizes what is really a modeling problem. If direction 1 lands, the pressure mostly evaporates. Don't build now.

### B2 intersection with A3 (Spec-Ack trailer)

Two touchpoints. First, the trailer is today the only churn-free clearing tool for fan-out, and the incident used it as a whole-diff blanket downgrade of a code — which maximizes the blast radius of any durability or authorship hole A3 finds (Trailer.read/2 unions git log base..HEAD, trailer.ex:55-61; cooperative self-report with no authorship check per the moduledoc, trailer.ex:20-23). Second, if acknowledgment were redesigned around bindings (candidate 3), that redesign lives inside the trailer grammar and inherits A3's durability semantics wholesale — another reason to prefer the severity split, which moves acknowledgment pressure back to honest per-subject spec edits for a small primary set.

## B3. Trailing slash in lib_paths (ticket ancora-ufm)

### The two disagreeing rules

- Tolerant side: Ancora.ChangeAnalysis.under_lib_path?/2, lib/ancora/change_analysis.ex:30-35 — does String.trim_trailing(lib_path, "/") then prefix-match, so `lib_paths: ["src/"]` matches src/thing.ex and the file is in scope for change/uncovered_file.
- Strict side: Ancora.Derive.ModuleLocator.source_path?/2, lib/ancora/derive/module_locator.ex:155-160 — no trim; `String.starts_with?(path, lib_path <> "/")` tests against "src//", never matches, so the file is never indexed as source and can never enter any subject footprint.

So the finding fires and doing what it asks (tag a test that covers the file) cannot clear it, because footprint membership is decided by the strict rule. String.trim_trailing appears exactly once in all of lib/, in the tolerant helper; nothing upstream normalizes.

### Did commit 7511407 fix it?

No — it INTRODUCED the tolerant half. 7511407 (2026-09-03, the ancora-p47 stack) replaced the hardcoded `PolicyFiles.classify == :lib` filter with under_lib_path?/2. source_path?/2 predates it and was outside that ticket's allowed touches. The disagreement is live on main right now.

### The class is wider than uncovered_file

HEAD sources come from Path.wildcard (module_locator.ex:51-58), where Path.join collapses the doubled slash, so the HEAD side tolerates a trailing slash. The base side filters prefetched base blobs through strict source_path?/2 (module_locator.ex:88), so with a trailing slash, changed base sources get dropped. Base and head module sets then diverge for reasons unrelated to the diff, and that feeds membership, def-indexes, and drift/growth/shrink comparison — not just footprints.

### B3 candidate directions

1. Normalize at load time in ProjectInfo.validate_lib_paths/1 (lib/ancora/project_info.ex:138-147) — recommended. Every source of lib_paths funnels through it: explicit opts (line 116), .spec/config.yml via configured_lib_paths (line 124), and the elixirc_paths fallback (line 131). Trim there, then delete the trim in under_lib_path?/2 so exactly one place owns normalization. Kills the whole class, including the base/head divergence, in a few lines.
2. Shared boundary helper (the ticket auditor's suggestion): one under_path?/2 used by both call sites. Worth having so prefix-matching has one spelling, but strictly weaker — the next consumer has to remember it exists. Complement, not the fix.
3. Reject trailing slashes at config parse with a config/invalid_value finding. User-hostile for input with an obvious canonical form. Skip.

## Architect-facing summary

All three findings are one disease: the trigger rule and the clearing rule are computed from different models, so a correct diff cannot satisfy the finding. B1's missing_decision fires on diff path sets (policy_files.ex:114-117) while the corpus already carries real governance linkage — spec `decisions:` frontmatter (schema/meta.ex:12) and ADR `affects:` resolution (decision_parser/affects.ex) — that the gate never consults; the transcript shows an orchestrator wrongly ruling that frontmatter clears it, a worker proving it path-only from source, and the "fix" being exactly the noise ADR edit the rule incentivizes ("S1 passed cleanly only because its diff happened to carry four decision files"). Cheapest honest rule: per changed spec, suppress when its `decisions:` names a resolving ADR whose `affects:` names it back; keep co-change only for the frontmatter-less governance files. B2's drift is computed per subject over transitive footprints with no primary-subject concept, so seven changed functions became 46 errors on 25 untouched subjects and blocked a pipeline 5h20m awaiting a human Spec-Ack ruling; the authored `surface:` field (216/216 atlas subjects, parsed, used nowhere) supports a primary/transitive split — a derived/drift_transitive code defaulting to info cuts Telemetry.metrics/0 from 26 errors to 6 and composes with every severity mechanism because they all key on code. That route also takes pressure off the Spec-Ack trailer (A3's subject): today it is the only churn-free clearing tool and the incident used it as a whole-diff blanket downgrade; binding-scoped ack grammar is the over-engineered alternative and would inherit A3's durability semantics wholesale. B3 is two prefix rules disagreeing about trailing slashes — change_analysis.ex:30-35 trims, module_locator.ex:155-160 doesn't — and commit 7511407 introduced the tolerant half rather than fixing anything; normalizing once in ProjectInfo.validate_lib_paths/1, the single funnel all lib_paths sources flow through, kills the class including a subtler base/head source-set divergence that contaminates drift comparison, not just footprints.

# Findings C — Expressiveness gaps (ancora-gg8)

Repos read: ancora (main @ 7511407), specled_ex, atlas (main @ 92fd890af plus branch atlas-1f8). Sessions read: 98be5781, 7f2b6af7, 85679cb0 under ~/.claude-remembers/projects/-Users-mz-dev-mz-atlas/.

## C1. No command verification kind

### Root cause

Ancora 1.0 retired every verification kind except tagged_tests as a charter decision, and shipped no replacement recipe for the one thing kind: command was actually used for in the field: repository-text gates ("this token must never appear in these files").

- The retirement is deliberate: ancora.decision.no_execution_no_state (/Users/mz/src/ancora/.spec/decisions/ancora.decision.no_execution_no_state.md:15-31) names the defect class, "repo-authored shell ran from a 'read-only' task", and decrees "No ancora task executes tests or repository shell. The only subprocess is git."
- command is in the retired list at /Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/schema/verification.ex:9-12; a spec still carrying it gets format/retired_construct (warning) from /Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/parser.ex:181-195.
- A requirement whose only cover was a command gate falls to spec/requirement_unverified at info (/Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/verifier.ex:128-154, default at /Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/finding.ex:64).
- The migration doc maps old finding codes (/Users/mz/src/ancora/docs/migration.md:53-54) but says nothing about what a working command gate should become. That silence is the gap consumers are filling by hand.

### What specled's command kind actually was

Schema: kind: command, target = a shell string, covers, plus an execute flag (/Users/mz/src/specled_ex/lib/specled_ex/schema/verification.ex:7-17). Execution was double-gated: --run-commands on the CLI AND execute: true in the spec (/Users/mz/src/specled_ex/lib/specled_ex/verifier.ex:20,380). Without both, the "verification" was only a non-empty-string check (verifier.ex:759-769) — a command gate nobody ran still counted as coverage.

The execution machinery is the tell for why it died. run_command/4 (verifier.ex:2335-2419) writes two wrapper scripts to temp files (an OTP erl_child_setup fd-retention workaround, per specled.decision.tempfile_command_execution), needs setsid on Linux but set -m on macOS to get a killable process group, SIGKILLs the group on timeout, truncates output to 2KB head+tail in findings, and re-parses ExUnit seeds out of the output so flakes are reproducible (verifier.ex:627-698). That is hundreds of lines of portability and forensics code to run arbitrary repo-authored shell from a gate that advertises itself as read-only — and the result was still machine-dependent (PATH, shell, installed tools) and sandbox-hostile. The ADR's claim that each capability "bought a class of defects" is borne out by the code.

### What consumers did instead, and how it compares

Atlas lost two grep gates in the migration. Session 98be5781, 2026-09-03T02:58Z:

"Ancora supports only tagged-test verification, so the two grep-based command gates this epic added under graph access scoping (no tier in retrieval, no payload bytes in code-access logs) had to be dropped, as main dropped its own. The requirements and scenarios survive; the payload-bytes requirement now reads as unverified at info level until a tagged test replaces the grep."

The same session hand-ported the payload-bytes gate to an ExUnit source-scan test at ~08:26Z, landed as atlas commit c84d727ff (/Users/mz/dev/mz/atlas/test/atlas/graph/access_scoping_logs_test.exs). Two later sessions independently adopted the pattern as convention: 7f2b6af7 (~16:18Z, next epic's plan: "The retrieval tripwire becomes an ExUnit source scan covering both the tier and the new field") and 85679cb0 (~19:24Z, "a tripwire test that fails if any retrieval file ever reads the disclosure field"). Three sessions, one day, same hand-rolled solution.

Honest comparison, command kind vs the ExUnit source-scan test:

- Determinism: command was machine-dependent shell (PATH, tool versions, OS shell semantics); the scan is a pure File.read! of the working tree, byte-identical everywhere.
- Spec integration: command had its own covers: channel; the scan gets it free — @tag spec: marks the requirement verified through the existing tagged_covers path.
- Gate semantics: command ran only under --run-commands + execute: true, and an unexecuted command still counted as coverage; with the scan, ancora proves the tag exists and mix test in CI proves it passes — the same trust model as every other tagged test.
- Failure reporting: command gave exit code plus 2KB truncated output in a finding; the scan gives a full ExUnit assertion naming file:line per violation, colocated with the scanner.
- Sandbox/CI: command meant arbitrary shell from the gate task with per-OS process-group kill hacks; the scan needs nothing new, it is just a test.
- Expressiveness: command could say whatever grep can; the scan can say whatever Elixir can — the atlas port is deliberately WIDER than the grep it replaced (test moduledoc lines 11-14: the old pattern "only caught the inspect(payload) spelling, so Logger.debug interpolating content slipped through it").
- Authoring cost: command was one YAML line; the scan is ~100 lines of scanner per gate (balanced-paren walker, interpolation extraction, string stripping) plus a hand-written vacuity guard (refute files == [], test lines 44-45).

The pattern won on every dimension except authoring cost. That last row is the whole remaining problem: each session re-derives the scanner and the vacuity guard from scratch, and a hand-rolled scanner without the vacuity guard is a silent green.

### Options

(a) Reinstate kind: command. Contradicts the charter ADR, re-imports the tempfile/process-group/timeout machinery, and reintroduces repo-authored shell into the "read-only" gate — the exact trust regression 1.0 is sold on removing. The unexecuted-command-counts-as-coverage hole comes back too. No.

(b) Bless the ExUnit source-scan pattern officially. Document it as THE replacement in docs/migration.md and the spec-led skills, with a copyable template that bakes in the two things people get wrong: the vacuity guard and whole-token matching (the atlas test's negative-lookaround regex, line 38). Optionally a tiny shared helper — ancora is already a dep of the consumer, so an Ancora.SourceScan test-support module (scan dirs, token list, allowlist, vacuity refute) would collapse each gate to ~15 declarative lines. Start with the documented template; ship the helper only if copy-paste drift shows up.

(c) A declarative built-in ("forbidden pattern" the gate checks itself). Charter-compatible in the narrow sense — the verifier already reads target files, and a pure file scan is not execution. But it recreates exactly the weak-grep semantics the atlas port improved past (a regex can't tell a binding from a string literal), needs new schema, matching semantics, coverage semantics, docs, and a second verification vocabulary one release after distilling to one kind. The evidence says the value of these gates comes from being smarter than a pattern. YAGNI.

Recommendation: (b), minimal form. The convention is already load-bearing in the flagship consumer; the cheapest trust win is making the third session's hand-rolled port unnecessary, not adding gate machinery. Zero ancora-core code required for the first step.

## C2. Overrides scope to a subject, not a requirement

### Root cause

The override grammar's match key is (subject, code) because the Finding struct throws requirement identity away, so there is nothing narrower to match against — even though every requirement-scoped finding creation site already has the requirement id in hand.

- Config.Override carries subject, code, severity, reason only (/Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/config.ex:32-42); matching is ovr.subject == subject and ovr.code == code (config.ex:163-167).
- Finding keeps code, subject, file, message, severity, severity_source (/Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/finding.ex:11-18). The :requirement key is accepted by Finding.new but used only to render the message (finding.ex:139,159), then dropped.
- The creation sites pass it: requirement: req_id at /Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/verifier.ex:144 (spec/requirement_unverified) and /Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/tag_findings.ex:100,157 (tags/requirement_untagged, tags/new_requirement_untagged).
- Severity resolution threads only finding.subject into the config lookup: gate (/Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/gate.ex:351) → Severity.resolve_all → resolve_finding puts :subject (/Users/mz/src/ancora/lib/ancora/severity.ex:143-148) → Config.severity_for(config, code, subject) (config.ex:145-150).

No ADR defends subject scope. ancora.findings.per_subject_overrides (/Users/mz/src/ancora/.spec/specs/ancora.findings.spec.md:118-126, stability: evolving) specifies it, but records no requirement-vs-subject deliberation. Subject was simply the only identity the Finding struct retained. This is an accident of struct shape, not a design position.

### Consumer evidence

Atlas needed to silence tags/new_requirement_untagged for exactly one requirement (S5 of tier_is_disclosure, blocked until an enforce-flip lands in prod) and had to take the whole subject. /Users/mz/dev/mz/atlas/.spec/config.yml, in the override's own reason field:

"The override grammar scopes to a subject, not a requirement, so this is as narrow as Ancora 1.0 allows. Remove it when S5 lands."

Session 98be5781 at 08:23Z shows the intent was requirement-scoped from the start: "a narrowly scoped override for the S5 requirement with its reason and a removal condition." The grammar widened it. Blast radius is real: mcp.code_access_tools.spec.md holds 34 ids, and the overridden code is the one that warns when a NEW requirement lands untagged — on the disclosure gate's own subject, the worst possible place to mute it. Every requirement added to that subject until S5 lands slips to info silently.

### Cost of requirement-scoped overrides

Small and contained; every piece already has the data flowing past it:

1. Finding: add optional :requirement field (finding.ex:11-18,135-142) — creation sites need no change, they already pass it.
2. Severity.resolve_finding: also put finding.requirement into opts (severity.ex:145).
3. Config.Override: optional requirement field; matching becomes ovr.requirement in [nil, finding_requirement] on top of today's check (config.ex:163-167). An entry without requirement: behaves exactly as today, so existing configs are untouched.
4. parse_override_entry: accept optional requirement, validate against known claim ids the way subject is validated against known_subjects (config.ex:392-465).
5. Spec + docs: widen ancora.findings.per_subject_overrides (additive — an optional narrowing key downgrades nothing; append-only safe) and the Config moduledoc (config.ex:11-16).

subject_status/2 (config.ex:156-159) labels a subject acknowledged when any override names it; a requirement-scoped override should still count, so no change there. Only meaningful design question: which codes accept requirement:. Cheapest honest answer: any override may carry it; it simply never matches findings that have no requirement. Extra validation (rejecting requirement: on codes that never set one) is more machinery than it earns right now.

Recommendation: do it. The fix is smaller than the workaround — the atlas reason block spends three lines apologizing for the grammar.

## Architect summary

C1: ancora dropped kind: command on purpose, and the no_execution_no_state ADR is right — specled's tempfile/setsid/process-group execution stack is the proof. What 1.0 forgot is that command gates had one dominant use (forbidden-text tripwires) and the migration doc offers no successor, so atlas sessions invented one: ExUnit source-scan tests. The invention is better than what it replaced — deterministic, tag-integrated, and strictly wider than the old grep (it catches interpolated bindings the grep missed) — and three sessions in one day independently converged on it. Don't reinstate command, and don't build a declarative pattern-check (it would recreate weak-grep semantics plus new schema). Bless the pattern: a documented template in migration.md and the spec-led skills carrying the vacuity guard and whole-token regex, with a small Ancora.SourceScan test helper as an optional second step. Near-zero engineering for the trust gained.

C2: overrides match (subject, code) only because the Finding struct drops the requirement id its creation sites already supply — an accident of struct shape, with no ADR behind it. Atlas wanted to override one blocked requirement (S5) and was forced to mute tags/new_requirement_untagged across a 34-id subject, on the disclosure gate itself, with an apology in the reason field. The fix is an optional requirement: key on override entries: five small edits (Finding field, one line in Severity, Override match, config parse + validation, docs/spec), fully backward-compatible. The fix is smaller than the workaround. Do it.
